items.text: A collection of movements, often based on dances. Listen for a shared key and changes of metre, pulse and character between movements.
Usually a measured dance in duple metre. Follow its flowing subdivisions and the way a short opening figure passes through the texture.
Related dance names with different French and Italian practices. French courantes often play with the grouping of beats; Italian correnti tend toward running motion.
Often a slow triple-metre dance. Listen for weight on the second beat and for dissonances that ask to be held before resolving.
A lively closing dance, frequently in compound metre. Imitation may make each hand seem to answer the other.
A subject enters in successive voices. Identify its shape first; an answer or later entry can change register, key or surrounding material.
Opening or exploratory forms. Their freedom does not mean an absence of structure: listen for recurring figures, bass patterns and harmonic arrivals.
Recurring ensemble material separated by contrasting episodes. Returns may be shortened or placed in a new key.
Repeated bass or harmonic patterns support changing upper parts. Keep the repetition in mind while listening for what is transformed.
A trill, mordent or other sign can belong to the written language of a piece. MIDI does not always expand those signs into performed notes.
Concerto contrast, melodic sequences and clear bass support are useful starting points. Italian composers and their music travelled widely; the label is not a nationality test.
Dance types, notes inégales, agréments and the overture are recurring concerns. Their realization depends on the piece and source; this player does not impose a universal French performance rule.
Contrapuntal writing, chorale settings and the organ tradition intersect with French and Italian models. The label covers varied courts, churches and cities.
Iberian keyboard genres and English virginal, theatre and church music have distinct histories. Compare an actual source piece rather than treating either region as one sound.
These period divisions are broad teaching aids. Composers and works can cross them; the catalogue retains overlapping periods.
Bach’s sons and other later figures introduce galant and empfindsam approaches. Their inclusion shows continuity and change rather than extending one style indefinitely.
Mute the other tracks. Notice where the bass moves and where it rests. Then bring one upper line back.
Solo a voice, hear its phrase, then use All together. Ask what becomes clearer or harder to follow in the complete texture.
Set A before an entry and B after its answer. Slow the passage without changing pitch. Remove the loop when its shape becomes familiar.
Use the exact-title YouTube search link. Compare timing, articulation and ornaments with the local synthesis. The player is a reading aid, not a historical-performance claim.
